Empirical Research Plan – “Investor Sentiment and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns”

---------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) in panel data.

Rationale  
• Two natural dimensions of variation exist:  
  (i) Time: sentiment fluctuates from year to year.  
  (ii) Cross-section: some firms are ex-ante “hard to value / hard to arbitrage” (HV) whereas others are “easy to value” (EV).  
• A DiD design compares the ex-post returns of HV vs. EV firms following high-sentiment (“optimism”) years to the same difference following low-sentiment (“pessimism”) years.  
• Firm and year fixed effects absorb unobserved, time-invariant firm traits and common macro shocks.  
• Because the six sentiment proxies are pre-whitened with respect to macro fundamentals, and because sentiment is measured at t (prior to the return window t+1 … t+12), reverse causality is unlikely.

---------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• HighSent_t  = 1 if the composite sentiment index in fiscal year t is in its top tercile (alternatively above 0 after standardisation); 0 otherwise.  
• HV_i        = 1 if firm i belongs to the top tercile for at least FOUR of the following seven characteristics measured at t-1:  
  – Small size (ME)  
  – Young age  
  – High idiosyncratic volatility (sigma)  
  – Negative profitability (E/BE<0)  
  – Non-dividend payer  
  – Extreme growth (lowest BM quintile OR top sales-growth decile)  
  – Financially distressed (top O-score decile)  
• Treated observation: HV_i =1 & HighSent_t =1.

Control groups  
1. Pure time counterfactual: HV firms in LOW-sentiment years (HV_i =1 & HighSent_t =0).  
2. Pure cross-section counterfactual: EV firms in the SAME high-sentiment years (HV_i =0 & HighSent_t =1).  
3. Difference-in-Differences benchmark: EV firms in low-sentiment years (baseline).  

Treatment timing / event date  
• Sentiment is observed at the end of June of year t, using only information through June.  
• Outcome window: monthly excess returns from July of year t to June of year t+1 (following the established July-to-June matching convention).  

No running variable or cutoff is needed (not RDD).

---------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends  
In the absence of sentiment shocks, the return spread between HV and EV firms would evolve similarly across high- and low-sentiment years.  
Plausibility: Both groups are exposed to common macro factors; firm & year FE plus factor-model controls (Mkt-RF, SMB, HML, MOM) further align trends. Parallel-trend diagnostics can be run using leads of the sentiment dummy.

A2. Exogeneity of sentiment relative to future returns  
The (orthogonalised) sentiment index at year-t is not affected by yet-unrealised t+1 returns; mechanical timing helps, and the use of macro-orthogonalised principal components mitigates confounding by fundamentals.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)  
A high-sentiment wave does not alter the risk exposures of EV firms in ways that differentially change their expected returns solely because HV firms are also treated. Given the breadth of U.S. equity markets, spillovers are unlikely to create large cross-sectional contamination within one year.

---------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
---------------------------------------------------------
T1. Time-varying risk, not sentiment, drives return differences  
• Mitigation: Control for Fama-French-Carhart factor betas estimated pre-t, include firm-specific risk controls (βMKT, βSMB, βHML, βMOM) interacted with HighSent_t.  

T2. Measurement error/classification error in HV status  
• Mitigation: (i) Use multiple alternative HV definitions (simple size*BM criterion, continuous “speculative intensity” index). (ii) Show that re-classifying borderline firms does not change results.  

T3. Macroeconomic states correlated with sentiment and heterogeneous across firms  
• Mitigation: (i) Add year-level controls: real GDP growth, Fed funds rate, NBER recessions, oil shocks. (ii) Use sentiment residuals already orthogonalised to macro series. (iii) Conduct sub-sample analyses inside expansions and recessions separately.

---------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ----------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional fixed effects
library(lubridate)
library(broom)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ----------------------------------------------------
crsp  <- fread("crsp_monthly.csv")      # firm-month returns
comp  <- fread("compustat_annual.csv")  # accounting vars
sent  <- fread("sentiment_annual.csv")  # year t composite index
mac   <- fread("macro_controls.csv")    # GDP, FF rate, recession dummy

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# ----------------------------------------------------
## 2.1 Fiscal year alignment: keep vars from t-1 for returns July t -> June t+1
comp[, fy_end := ymd(fy_end)]
comp[, year_ret := year(fy_end) + 1]  # July of following calendar year
crsp[, year_ret := ifelse(month(date) >= 7, year(date), year(date) - 1)]

## 2.2 Merge firm-year characteristics to monthly returns
dat <- merge(crsp, comp, by = c("permno","year_ret"))
dat <- merge(dat, sent,  by.x = "year_ret", by.y = "year")
dat <- merge(dat, mac,   by.x = "year_ret", by.y = "year")

## 2.3 Construct HV dummy
# Indicator variables
dat[, small := (rank(market_equity, ties.method="first")/.N) <= 0.33, by = year_ret]
dat[, young := age <= 3]
dat[, high_sigma := (rank(sigma, ties.method="first")/.N) >= 0.67, by = year_ret]
dat[, unprof := E_BE < 0]
dat[, no_div := payer_dummy == 0]
dat[, growth := (rank(book_to_market, ties.method="first")/.N) <= 0.2, by = year_ret]
dat[, distress := (rank(oz_sc, ties.method="first")/.N) >= 0.9, by = year_ret]

dat[, hv_count := small + young + high_sigma + unprof + no_div + growth + distress]
dat[, HV := as.integer(hv_count >= 4)]

## 2.4 Treatment dummy
dat[, HighSent := as.integer(sentiment_std > 0)]      # standardised index > 0
dat[, Treat := HV * HighSent]

## 2.5 Outcome variables
dat[, excess_ret := ret - rf]                         # monthly excess return
dat[, ln1p_ret := log(1 + excess_ret)]                # log form

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DiD Regression (firm & year FE, clustered by year)
# ----------------------------------------------------
reg_main <- feols(ln1p_ret ~ HV*HighSent + 
                    mkt_rf + smb + hml + mom |
                    permno + year_ret,
                  data = dat, cluster = "year_ret")
summary(reg_main)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 4. Pre-trend / Lead Test
# ----------------------------------------------------
dat[, HighSent_lead1 := shift(HighSent, n = -1, type="lag"), by = permno]
pretrend <- feols(ln1p_ret ~ HV*HighSent_lead1 |
                    permno + year_ret,
                  data = dat, cluster = "year_ret")
summary(pretrend)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness – Continuous Sentiment Interaction
# ----------------------------------------------------
reg_cont <- feols(ln1p_ret ~ HV:sentiment_std + sentiment_std |
                    permno + year_ret,
                  data = dat, cluster = "year_ret")
summary(reg_cont)

# ----------------------------------------------------
# 6. Export tidy table
# ----------------------------------------------------
library(modelsummary)
modelsummary(list(Main = reg_main, Lead = pretrend, Continuous = reg_cont))
```

---------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that sentiment-driven mispricing inflates (deflates) HV stock prices during optimism (pessimism), so subsequent returns should be abnormally low (high). Therefore:

β₁ (HV × HighSent) ≈ –0.50% to –0.80% per month (-6 to ‑10 % per year) on log returns.  
Economic magnitude: roughly twice the average monthly market risk premium, large enough to be of practical relevance.

---------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DiD)
---------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends documented                               … 1  
C2. No anticipation / reverse causality (timing, leads)          … 1  
C3. No spillovers or interference                                 … 0.5 (cannot fully rule out)  
C4. Stable composition of treatment & control groups             … 0.5 (entry/exit of firms)  
C5. Robustness to alternative specifications & placebo tests     … 1  
Total score: 4 / 5

---------------------------------------------------------
End of Research Plan
